source.title: Multi-Epoch learning with Data Augmentation for Deep Click-Through Rate Prediction
source.authors: Zhongxiang Fan; Zhao-Cheng Liu; Jian Liang; Dongying Kong; Han Li; Peng Jiang; Shuang Li; Kun Gai

record.file_problem: none; full paper text is present
record.tranche_reason: The paper measures test performance over epochs in deep CTR models and reports early overfitting, as well as settings where it is mitigated. Its results refine the epoch-wise claim but do not establish the full fall-rise-fall curve.
record.gate_note: The paper tests epoch-wise test performance, primarily with test AUC. Its Figure 2 directly compares ordinary multi-epoch training (Direct) with MEDA. It also reports single-epoch versus two-epoch MEDA AUC results in Tables 2 and 3. Figure-only curves are recorded as such. The paper does not test model-size sweeps, interpolation thresholds, sample-size effects near such a threshold, effective complexity, label noise, regularization tuning, or parameter-count remeasurement. Cited results from other studies are not extracted as rows.
record.test_reason: The paper never mentions double descent; it studies one-epoch overfitting in CTR models. Only its Direct multi-epoch test-AUC curves (Fig. 2) record ordinary epoch-wise test performance in deep networks, the quantity V2 names. Test AUC falls from epoch 2 with no reported recovery, but the window is only 8 epochs. All other results concern the authors' MEDA method or its ablations.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors conclude that one-epoch overfitting in CTR models stems from embedding-layer overfitting caused by high-dimensional sparsity. Their MEDA method (reinitializing or using multiple independent embeddings per epoch) lets multi-epoch training beat single-epoch training (test AUC +0.8% to 4.6% on public data) without overfitting, acts as data augmentation, and helps in an online A/B test. They do not frame any result in double-descent terms.
record.recipe_differences: The study evaluates ordinary direct multi-epoch CTR training and its own embedding-reinitialization/data-augmentation approaches; it does not reproduce the original double-descent methods or measurements.
record.method_sensitivity: The temporal outcome changes with training method and embedding handling: Direct training declines from epoch 2 in the public-data plots; MEDA improves across epochs in most reported models; embedding-reuse continual variants overfit beyond epoch 10.

fits_no_version.finding: In sparse-embedding CTR models, ordinary multi-epoch training degrades test AUC from epoch 2 onward (one-epoch overfitting). Ablations attribute this to the embedding layer, not the MLP.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: One-epoch overfitting in high-dimensional sparse CTR models arises from embedding-layer overfitting, and test performance does not recover within ~8 epochs.

record.problems: The direct epoch-wise evidence is presented as curves without extracted numerical values. Many other results are comparisons of one versus two epochs, not full temporal sweeps. The paper does not establish a complete fall-rise-fall curve for ordinary training, and the main multi-epoch improvement results use the proposed MEDA intervention.
record.rows_left_out: No rows omitted from the extracted epoch-wise results. Sample-rate tables were not treated as V3 results because they do not test increasing data near an interpolation threshold; epoch counts there are reported as the counts needed to reach a reference AUC.

untested.parts: Whether test error re-descends after the epoch-2 rise; ordinary training is shown only to epoch 8, with no label noise and no long-horizon curve.
Data-keeping-rate tables (4,5) use MEDA and report epochs needed to reach a reference AUC; no sample-size sweep near an interpolation threshold.
No label-noise or regularization-tuning manipulation; weight decay and dropout are only cited as ineffective from prior work.

record.verdict_notes: The record's two limits_scope labels are removed. The MEDA and ablation rows are the authors' own interventions, not natural training dynamics. The Direct curves cover only 8 epochs, so they cannot show whether a second descent would follow. The rise after epoch 1 alone neither supports nor challenges V2. Fig. 2 does not name the models it uses. The paper cites Belkin et al. only in passing, in a list of overfitting work. A reviewer might reasonably reclassify this study as T6/cites_only.

versions.untested_parts: Model-size sweep and peak near the size that just fits training data.
The paper reports epoch-wise performance and early overfitting, but does not establish the full fall-rise-fall shape or a later second descent for ordinary training.
No test of increasing sample size near an interpolation threshold and its effect on test error.
No general double-descent test across model classes.
No unified effective-complexity measure or test of whether it predicts peak locations.
No test of noise or regularization as drivers of the peak, multiple descent peaks, or disappearance under optimal regularization.
No re-counting of complexity by effective parameter count.

relation.reason: Figure 2 measures ordinary deep-network test performance across epochs, bearing on V2 despite the paper not explicitly discussing double descent.

tranche.reason: Direct-training epoch curves provide results on V2 in a CTR setting. The limited training window does not establish that V2 is wrong or requires qualification.

source_check.notes: Direct-training AUC declines from epoch 2; no later recovery is reported within epochs 1–8, leaving V2 undetermined. MEDA comparisons and intervention ablations should not serve as claim-evidence rows.

reader_labels.reason: Test AUC drops from the second epoch, documenting early overfitting but not the later recovery required for the full curve (r25–r26).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: MEDA training and reported two-epoch comparisons
reader_labels.reason: MEDA generally improves test AUC across epochs or from one to two epochs, while some MEDA variants overfit; the temporal pattern depends on training method and the full curve is not established (r1–r24, r27–r45).
